claims.text: A tailored thermomechanical route combining controlled deformation with annealing or quenching can improve the targeted mechanical-property combination in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed processing route will induce a fine-scale dual-phase microstructure with uniformly distributed nanoscale interfaces.
Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys generally have coarse, homogeneous, single-phase microstructures.
Controlled deformation followed by calibrated annealing or quenching can form fine precipitates, nanotwins, or dual-phase lamellae in situ.
Precise control of deformation degree, cooling rate, annealing temperature, and annealing time is required for the method to work.
The method is expected to work for high-entropy-alloy compositions amenable to controlled phase separation.
Formation of brittle intermetallic phases or departure from the optimal processing window may negate the mechanical-property improvements.
Nanoscale precipitates, twins, and interphase boundaries act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
A refined dual-phase microstructure with nanoscale interfaces suppresses strain localization.
Precipitation and interface hardening increase strength by blocking dislocations.
The generated nanoscale features improve ductility by promoting more uniform plastic deformation.
The generated microstructural features improve fracture resistance by mitigating crack propagation.
The processed alloy will exhibit a significant increase in yield strength relative to a conventionally processed alloy.
The processed alloy will maintain or slightly improve ductility relative to a conventionally processed alloy.
The processed alloy will have a comparable or higher Young's modulus.
The processed alloy will exhibit increased fracture toughness.
Conventionally thermally processed high-entropy alloys typically have lower strength-ductility synergy than alloys receiving the combined processing route.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition and processing control.
Failure to obtain statistically significant simultaneous improvements in all four targeted properties, or failure to observe the intended microstructure, would falsify the hypothesis.
